title: The news
hook: how to take in the world without despair: Jesus and the tower of Siloam, Epictetus and what's in our power
tomorrow: a herdsman told a temple to turn off its music. why?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: my corner. Daniel's window was open, as it was aforetime. Today the window lets the whole world in.

The feed refreshes: a flood, a crash, a cruelty, all before breakfast. Luke's Gospel has people arriving with the news of their own day. Some tell Jesus about Galileans killed by the Roman governor, Galileans "whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices." And Jesus brings up another headline himself: eighteen people killed when the tower in Siloam fell on them. Two disasters, one cruel and one an accident. What do you do with news like that?
screen: `A FLOOD, A CRASH, BEFORE BREAKFAST.` → `THE NEWS FROM PILATE.` → `THE TOWER IN SILOAM.`

segments.voice: His answer turns twice. First he refuses the easy reading: "Suppose ye that these Galilaeans were sinners above all the Galilaeans, because they suffered such things? I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish." The victims weren't worse people. The news isn't a verdict on them. Then he turns the listeners back to their own lives: change your own heart. Christians hear in it a call to turn toward God, not to judge the people in the headline. A neighbor tradition says something close in its own words. The Stoic teacher Epictetus opens his Handbook: "Of things some are in our power, and others are not." Our judgments and our choices are ours; the world's events are not. Here's what they share: both send you back from the headline to what's yours to do. And the honest difference: Jesus turns the listener toward God and repentance, a change of heart. Epictetus turns you toward your own judgments, with reason as the guide. Awake to the world, not drowning in it.
screen: `THE NEWS IS NOT A VERDICT ON THEM.` · `TURN TO YOUR OWN LIFE.` · `SOME THINGS ARE IN OUR POWER.` · `REPENTANCE FOR ONE, REASON FOR THE OTHER.` · then, large: `AWAKE, NOT DROWNING.`

segments.voice: Pick one set time tomorrow for the news, and only one, and decide how long it gets. Then bring one of today's headlines to mind, name one small thing in it that's in your power, and let the rest go by with the breath.
The news: the world taken in at a set time, without judging its victims and without drowning. Siloam and the Handbook.
Here's the line: awake, not drowning, eyes open to the tower and feet on your own ground. See you out in the world.
